transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-31 16:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO - Luminark), Ethan Cole (Network Engineer), Marc Delaney (Head of Security), Sofia Kim (Product)

Auto-summary:
- Luminark is migrating sensitive inference workloads to an on-prem VPC gateway; priority is isolation, predictable latency, and auditability.
- Primary constraints: no internet egress from inference nodes except via managed NAT/egress appliance; need IP whitelisting, regional restrictions for EU data, and SOC2 evidence.

[00:00:05] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya Chen from Redwood. Quick around the room?
[00:00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya Rao here, CTO at Luminark. We're looking at moving inference off the public cluster and into our colo/VPC.
[00:00:20] Ethan: Ethan Cole, network, will be owning peering and routing.
[00:00:23] Marc: Marc Delaney, security, focused on compliance and key management.
[00:00:27] Sofia: Sofia Kim, product.
[00:00:30] Daniel: Daniel Ortiz, I'm Redwood's solutions engineer, happy to jump into the network details.

[00:01:05] Maya: Agenda is quick intro, then Daniel will walk through private deployment patterns — VPC peering, privatelink, transit gateway — and then Q&A.

[00:02:02] Daniel: Quick overview: Redwood supports three modes — hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private deployments. For private we do a control plane in the cloud and can deploy inference dataplane in your VPC or on-prem via private onramp. Two common patterns are: direct VPC peering / bgp (if both sides are cloud), or using PrivateLink / private endpoints where we create an endpoint service in your VPC and traffic stays internal. For on-prem you can do a transit-gateway/VPN or express route style connection into a VPC that hosts the dataplane, or you can run a customer-managed on-prem package.

[00:03:10] Ethan: Clarify — you said control plane in the cloud. Does that mean metadata goes out over the public internet?
[00:03:18] Maya: Good q. The control plane speaks to our API endpoints but all inference payloads can be pinned to the private dataplane — no user payload needs to leave the customer's network if you host dataplane privately. There are options to lock down egress so only management/control traffic leaves and that's over TLS back to our control plane.

[00:04:03] Marc: For SOC2 and audit we're going to need logs, KMS integration — customer-managed keys ideally — and an auditable chain for model access. Do you support HSM integrations?
[00:04:15] Daniel: Yes, Redwood Private supports KMS and can be configured to use customer-managed keys. HSM is via partner KMS/HSM integrations; we'll include a technical note. We also emit audit logs for token usage, model versions, rollouts, per-token latency — that's in the console.

[00:05:02] Priya: Our blocker is IP overlap — we run 10.0.0.0/8 across multiple sites. We need a plan so we don't cause collisions. Also we can't expose inference nodes to internet, only our NAT egress.
[00:05:20] Ethan: We prefer a model where Redwood instances get private IPs in our subnet and we control egress via our appliance, so all outbound goes through our firewall. Can you accommodate that?

[00:05:37] Daniel: Yes, that's typical. We can either peer the subnets directly so instances are in your VPC and use your NAT, or deploy in our VPC and use PrivateLink — with PrivateLink we present endpoints in your VPC so traffic is internal, and egress stays under your control. For on-prem colo, a VPN/DirectConnect into the VPC with route advertisement is common.

[00:06:40] Priya: What's the recommended approach for latency-sensitive workloads? We need p95 under 150ms for single-turn inference.
[00:06:51] Daniel: If you need strict latency, colocating the dataplane within your VPC or on-prem is best; avoid cross-region hops. We can run inference nodes in their region with GPU pinned capacity (Redwood Dedicated private dataplane) which minimizes path length. The tradeoff is cost and capacity planning.

[00:08:10] Marc: Data residency — some of our models and datasets must stay in EU. Can you run control plane in the US and dataplane in EU, and will that pass audit?
[00:08:25] Maya: Yes, many customers do split control vs dataplane. We can host dataplane exclusively in EU regions, and provide attestations and logs. We'll need to capture that as a requirement in the security packet.

[00:09:30] Ethan: On routing — how do you handle BGP and route advertisement? Can Redwood peer to our transit gateway?
[00:09:40] Daniel: We support BGP over VPN or Direct Connect. For cloud-to-cloud, peering to your transit gateway is supported; we can present routes and accept route propagation. We also support static route setups for simpler networks. There's sometimes an MTU and fragmentation nuance with large model payloads, we can share best-practices.

[00:10:55] Priya: About private endpoints — does the endpoint service need specific IP ranges?
[00:11:01] Daniel: The endpoints sit in your subnets. We ask for a /24 per endpoint as a guideline but it depends on scale. If you have overlapping address space we can ask you to carve dedicated prefixes or use NAT translation at the gateway. We'll send an IP planning worksheet.

[00:12:20] Sofia: For rollout — we want canary model updates and A/B tests but with audit. How are rollouts controlled when dataplane is customer-managed?
[00:12:31] Daniel: Rollouts are controlled via our console and rollout policies; if dataplane is private, the control plane still triggers rollouts but only after the customer dataplane checks pass. We can disable auto-updates and do manual canaries if that's preferred. All events are logged.

[00:13:50] Marc: Encryption at rest and in transit? We need TLS and disk-level encryption with our KMS.
[00:13:58] Daniel: TLS in transit always; for at-rest we can configure to use your KMS for disk encryption on nodes that hold cache or ephemeral model weights. If you need HSM-backed keys that's a conversation we can have with product security.

[00:15:10] Ethan: Egress IP requirements — we need static egress to allow third-party webhooks from our infra to whitelist. If Redwood runs in our VPC that's straightforward; if you run in your cloud we need a fixed egress set.
[00:15:24] Maya: We can provide a documented egress IP list if you're using Redwood-hosted dataplane but for private deployments customers prefer their own NAT. We'll include both options and the tradeoffs.

[00:16:40] Priya: Perf benchmarking — we'd like to run a realistic workload against your stack. We can bring a sample set of prompts. What's involved?
[00:16:50] Daniel: We'll set up a benchmark runbook: network topology, sample payloads, concurrency and token limits. Ideally we run from your environment into the private dataplane so we measure real e2e. I'll own assembling the runbook and sharing scripts.

[00:18:05] Marc: For compliance, we need SOC2, ISO docs and an explanation of retention for logs and model artifacts.
[00:18:15] Maya: We'll share the security packet (SOC2 report, ISO summaries, and our logging retention settings). For model artifacts retention you can control version retention and we can configure shorter retention for cached items.

[00:19:45] Ethan: One more — do you support mutual TLS between our clients and the dataplane?
[00:19:52] Daniel: Yes, mutual TLS and token-based auth are supported. You can also use SAML/Sso for user access to the console and RBAC for team separation.

[00:21:10] Sofia: Timeline — we're targeting a pilot in Q4. We'll need pricing for reserved capacity and private deployment.
[00:21:18] Maya: We'll provide a pilot proposal and capacity estimate. Pilot typically runs 4–6 weeks with a small footprint.

[00:22:30] Priya: Any limitations on model sizes or KV cache locality we should watch for?
[00:22:38] Daniel: Large models may require GPU nodes with higher memory; kv cache gets warmed in the same datacenter. If you plan for long context lengths we can recommend model quantization or sharded cache setups.

[00:24:05] Marc: Are there any known gotchas for on-prem colos? For instance, cross-connect latency or egress NAT saturating?
[00:24:15] Daniel: Yes, cross-connect oversubscription and NAT throughput are common issues. We'll review throughput requirements and recommend sizing guidelines; sometimes customers put a secondary NAT or deploy edge proxy for load shaping.

[00:26:00] Maya: Ok, recap and next steps. Action items: Daniel will share benchmark runbook; Maya will share network diagram and IP planning worksheet; Priya to send expected QPS and regions and compliance check list. We'll follow up with security packet and a pilot price estimate.
